title: Characterization of Helium Bubbles and Hydrogen/Tritium Interactions in Palladium Alloys Using Advanced Electron Microscopy
content: Understanding the nucleation and growth of helium (He) bubbles in palladium (Pd) alloys is crucial for optimizing the handling of nuclear fusion fuels deuterium and tritium [1, 2]. The formation of He bubbles can significantly impact the structural integrity and storage capacity of Pd, as these bubbles can lead to material embrittlement and degradation over time [3]. To predict how a material will age and perform over its service life, it is essential to understand how He atoms nucleate bubbles and the mechanisms by which metal atoms are displaced to accommodate the initial formation of these bubbles. Additionally, as more He atoms are generated with age, it is critical to determine whether bubbles grow through coalescence or other ripening mechanisms to understand long-term performance. Given the nanoscale size of He bubbles, advanced high-resolution electron microscopy techniques are essential for their characterization and quantification. However, the contrast from bubbles is small, and they have complex 3D distributions, necessitating advanced techniques to identify and label each bubble, its location relative to its neighbors, and its He content. These sophisticated imaging methods enable observation and analysis of the bubbles' formation, distribution, and growth dynamics, providing critical insights into the mechanisms that govern their behavior. This detailed understanding is vital for developing more durable and efficient Pd-based storage solutions, ensuring the safe and effective containment of hydrogen and its isotopes.
